summary.text: An enzyme is a biological macromolecule, usually a protein, that speeds up chemical reactions without being used up.
Enzymes lower a reaction's activation energy, often by factors of millions, and nearly all metabolic processes in a cell depend on them.
Each is highly specific because of its three-dimensional structure, and it can lose that structure and its function outside optimal conditions.

facts.label: First enzyme found
facts.value: Diastase, found by Anselme Payen in 1833

items.prompt: One enzyme helps convert many substrate molecules into product. What happens to the enzyme itself?

options.label: It is used up, one enzyme per reaction
It is regenerated at the end of each cycle
It becomes part of the final product
It shifts the reaction's equilibrium

items.explain: Like all catalysts, enzymes do not affect the overall equilibrium and are regenerated at the end of each cycle.

items.prompt: How does an enzyme make a reaction run faster?

options.label: It supplies extra heat to the reaction
It shifts the balance toward more product
It adds more substrate to the mix
It lowers the reaction's activation energy

items.explain: Enzymes increase the reaction rate by lowering activation energy, without changing the equilibrium.

items.prompt: A cook heats an enzyme-rich liquid far past its best conditions. What most likely happens to the enzymes?

options.label: They lose their structure and, with it, their function
They work faster the hotter it gets
They switch to catalysing different reactions
They turn into ribozymes

items.explain: Outside optimal conditions, enzymes may lose their structure through denaturation, leading to loss of function.

items.prompt: Lactase cleaves lactose, and DNA polymerase forms DNA polymers. What naming pattern do enzymes like these follow?

options.label: The discoverer's surname plus a number
The name of the organ where each is found
-ase attached to the substrate or the type of reaction
The date each was first isolated

items.explain: Enzymes are usually named by combining the suffix -ase with the name of the substrate or the type of reaction.

items.prompt: A scientist finds that sugar still ferments in a yeast extract even though no living yeast cells remain. What does this show?

options.label: Fermentation requires the life of the yeast cells
Fermentation can happen without living yeast
Sugar ferments by itself without any enzyme
Yeast extracts only ferment while still alive

items.explain: Buchner found that sugar was fermented by yeast extracts with no living cells in the mixture, earning a Nobel Prize for cell-free fermentation.

items.prompt: In the early 1900s some scientists doubted that proteins could catalyse reactions themselves. What eventually settled it?

options.label: Lysozyme was found in tears, saliva and egg whites
Yeast was shown to ferment sugar only while alive
Enzyme names were standardised using EC numbers
Pure proteins such as pepsin were shown to be enzymes

items.explain: Northrop and Stanley definitively demonstrated that pure proteins, such as pepsin, trypsin and chymotrypsin, can be enzymes.

paragraphs.heading: What an enzyme is
paragraphs.text: An enzyme is a large biological molecule, usually a protein, that works as a catalyst: it speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up. The molecules it acts on are its substrates, and it turns them into products. Almost every metabolic process in a cell needs enzymes to run at a useful speed, and a metabolic pathway is usually a series of enzyme-driven steps. Enzymes are known to catalyse more than 5,000 kinds of biochemical reaction.

paragraphs.heading: How they speed things up
paragraphs.text: Enzymes work by lowering a reaction's activation energy, often speeding it up by factors of millions. One enzyme, orotidine 5′-phosphate decarboxylase, turns a reaction that would otherwise take millions of years into one that takes milliseconds. Like all catalysts, enzymes do not shift a reaction's overall equilibrium, and they are restored at the end of each cycle.

paragraphs.heading: Picky and sensitive
paragraphs.text: What sets enzymes apart is how specific they are, a result of each one's particular three-dimensional shape. They are also sensitive to conditions such as temperature and pH. Outside their best conditions they can lose their shape, a change called denaturation, and stop working. Activators can boost their activity and inhibitors can reduce it, and many such substances act as drugs or poisons.

paragraphs.heading: From ferments to enzymes
paragraphs.text: By the late 1600s and early 1700s, people knew that stomach juices digest meat and that saliva and plant extracts turn starch into sugar, but not how. In 1833 the French chemist Anselme Payen discovered the first enzyme, diastase. Louis Pasteur later argued that yeast turns sugar into alcohol through a vital force that worked only inside living cells. In 1877 Wilhelm Kühne coined the word enzyme, from Greek meaning 'in yeast'.

paragraphs.heading: Life not required
paragraphs.text: Eduard Buchner, who published his first paper on yeast extracts in 1897, found that the extracts could ferment sugar even with no living yeast cells present. He called the responsible enzyme zymase and won the 1907 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Whether enzymes were proteins was still disputed; some argued proteins only carried the true enzymes. John Howard Northrop and Wendell Meredith Stanley settled it by showing that pure proteins, such as the digestive enzyme pepsin, can be enzymes.

paragraphs.heading: Seeing the shape
paragraphs.text: Because enzymes can be crystallized, their structures could eventually be worked out with x-ray crystallography. The first was lysozyme, which occurs in saliva, tears and egg whites and digests the coating of some bacteria; its structure was published in 1965. That result began the field of structural biology and the effort to see how enzymes work atom by atom.

paragraphs.heading: Names and numbers
paragraphs.text: Most enzyme names end in -ase and come from the substrate or the reaction: lactase cleaves lactose, and DNA polymerase builds DNA. Different enzymes that catalyse the same reaction are called isozymes. Each enzyme can also be given an EC number, a set of four numbers that runs from a broad class to a very specific activity.

paragraphs.heading: Enzymes at work for us
paragraphs.text: Enzymes are put to work outside living things too. Industry uses them to help produce antibiotics and other complex molecules. Biological washing powders contain enzymes that break down protein, starch and fat stains, and meat tenderizers use papain to break down proteins.
